coins.note: The start of the campaign, saved before the first day passed. Economy, estates, levies and the cabinet are not recorded: the game only settles them after a few monthly ticks. The Battle for the Strait has not begun yet.

Four and a half months in, three weeks after Morocco declared war on Castile. Granada is not in the war; Morocco can call us in under our alliance. Shares of power are estimated (tools/estate_power.py, calibrated on the 16 November reading); satisfaction comes from the save.
Shares of power are read off the estates screen at the moment of the save (the save itself doesn't hold them). Satisfaction and everything else come from the save.

Saved at the outbreak of Granada's first war, as the casus belli against Aragon was won; the declaration and the mustering of the host (Trent's account) come just after it. Shares of power are estimated (calibrated on 16 November 1337); a screen on 28 January 1339, with no save, showed the crown at 26.4%, so the crown may be underestimated here by a couple of points.

Three months into the war on Aragon, the day after the Ghuzāt al-Mujāhidīn event. Trent let the volunteers serve and hired their company just after this save (his account; the save shows the company, unhired, under Yaḥyā Raḥḥū at Gharnāṭa). Shares of power are estimated (calibrated on 16 November 1337); the Catalan merchant privileges have lapsed since that reading, so the nobles and burghers may be a little underestimated.

The day Uryūla fell, as Castile laid siege to Mursiyya and cut the road home (Trent's account). Both armies stand at Uryūla. Shares of power are estimated, calibrated on Trent's 2 May 1340 reading (the 1 May autosave); the nobility's satisfaction has fallen to 33.

The day of the peace with Aragon: thirteen locations ceded, from Balansiyya south, and war reparations for ten years. The dhimmī share is read off Trent's tooltip (140.53 of 961.60); the other shares are estimated and scaled to that screen's total.

coins.t: The ṭāʾifas of Balansiyya and Mursiyya
coins.note: Five days after Valencia and Murcia were released as ṭāʾifas. No month has turned since the peace, so income, expenses, estate satisfaction and the Strait read as on 11 August. Shares of power are estimated from the 11 August reading; with Valencia's Christians gone from Granada's own lands, the dhimmī share falls back and the nobility's rises.
Two days after Morocco's defeat: Castile now holds Runda, Marballa, al-Jazīra al-Khaḍrāʾ and Jabal Ṭāriq. Shares of power are estimated from the 11 August reading.
Shares of power are estimated from the 11 August 1340 reading. Ibn al-Khaṭīb is no longer at Granada's court: the save has him as a Castilian admiral.

Portugal is at war with itself, and its queen is the wife of the king of Castile. Shares of power are estimated from the 11 August 1340 reading, with the restored Catalan privileges and the Royal Decree folded in.

After the Jamāʿa of 1344: the Distribution of Power now favours the ruler and the royal harem is enshrined in the court's customs. Shares of power are estimated from the 11 August 1340 reading with both changes folded in; a fresh estates screen would test them.

coins.t: The debt paid down, the plague rumoured
coins.note: Autosave of 1 August 1346, the day the game opens the Black Death. The loans the save still holds come to 96 in principal; Trent's reading of the debt in August is 122. Shares of power are estimated from the 11 August 1340 reading; no law or privilege has changed since January 1345.

Two days after Morocco declared its war to reclaim al-Andalus on Castile, Portugal and Aragon, with Granada's call to arms unanswered. Shares of power are estimated from the 11 August 1340 reading; no law or privilege has changed since January 1345.

wars: The Second Moroccan War on Castile
coins.note: Granada has answered Morocco's call and stands at war with Castile, Portugal and Aragon; taking up arms against its overlord has suspended the tributary bond to Castile; the war will decide whether Granada keeps its independence. The Volunteers of the Faith have risen again under Yaḥyā Raḥḥū. Shares of power are estimated from the 11 August 1340 reading; no law or privilege has changed since January 1345.

wars: The Second Moroccan War on Castile
coins.note: Twenty months into the war with the three crowns: the Black Death has reached the realm, the amir has survived an attempt on his life, and Moroccan influence has passed Castile's for the first time. Granada still fights for its independence. Shares of power are estimated from the 11 August 1340 reading; no law or privilege has changed since January 1345.

Castile, broken by the plague, makes a separate peace with Granada alone. Granada takes 23 locations from Qurṭuba and Ishbīliyya to Jayyān and Úbeda, the Ṭāʾifa of Mursiyya receives the Murcia area, Castile pays reparations and annuls its treaties with Aragon, and Granada returns to the name of Castile's tributary. Shares of power are estimated from the 11 August 1340 reading; with the realm doubled in size they are rougher than usual.

The Mamlūk sultan answers the embassy to al-Qāhira with an alliance, soldiers and gold, and Granadan sovereignty stands above 50 again. Shares of power are calibrated on Trent's estates panel of 1 June 1349, three days before the save.

The Second Moroccan War ends. With Castile at the tipping point, Granada sold its promise not to fund the Marīnids for Qarmūna and the silver mines of Qusanṭīna (21 May); on 3 June Morocco surrendered to Castile, and the peace annulled Morocco's treaties with Granada. The Mamlūks remain the only ally. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

wars: The Revolt of the Kingdom of Sevilla
coins.note: The Castilian peasants of the new lands rise and declare a Kingdom of Sevilla, taking all 25 locations won in 1349 and 1351, Qurṭuba, Ishbīliyya, Jayyān and the silver of Qusanṭīna among them. Qashtāla, as overlord, takes the field on Granada's side. Granada is back to its 18 old locations. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

The revolt of the Kingdom of Sevilla is over. Granada crushed the rebel armies at Sharīsh and Shalūqa al-Kubrā before the Castilians could arrive, and at the peace Qashtāla reaffirmed the border of the Peace of Qurṭuba: all 25 locations return to Granada. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

The new lands held and calming: the governor seated at Qurṭuba, Duʿāʾ in the dīwān, the Powerful Harem, the jizya remitted, and a second Castilian rising stopped before it began. Sovereignty stands at 81. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading; the estates panel of 19 March 1355 (crown 32.4, nobility 26.2, ʿulamāʾ 7.0, burghers 10.7, commoners 4.1) agrees with them to within a point.

coins.t: The crowns at each other's throats
coins.note: Qashtāla and Portugal march on Arghūn, with Savoy and Sicily beside it, while Granada watches, its truce with Qashtāla running to 1363. Sovereignty stands at 98 and Morocco's influence at 2.6; Granada can now raise more men than Qashtāla. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

wars: The Marīnid War for the Submission of Granada
coins.note: Morocco declares war on Granada itself, under the Strait's casus belli to demand Andalusī submission, with Tlemcen, Tafilalt and Touat beside it; Qashtāla defends its tributary and Portugal comes in with Qashtāla, though Qashtāla has almost no men left after its war in Arghūn. Granadan sovereignty stands at 100. Khālid Raḥḥū sits in the dīwān. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

The day the truce with Qashtāla ends, Granada holds its casus belli (the game's reclaim al-Andalus) and goes to war for its independence. Qashtāla is still at war with Morocco, which holds 58 of its towns as far as Toledo; Aragon has come in on Qashtāla's side against Morocco, and Portugal has made its peace with Fās. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

Yūsuf I died on the march into Portugal on 1 August 1363, ten weeks into the War of Independence. Saʿd, fifteen, succeeds under the regency of Naṣr al-Istijjī, who has married the widowed Duʿāʾ. The treasury holds 24 against a deficit of 38 a month. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

Saʿd, of age since 18 January 1364, rules with two wives, Aiman the Mamlūk and Duʿāʾ the Marīnid. The Jamāʿa of May 1364 restored the dhimmī tax to win back the ʿulamāʾ. In the War of Independence his army broke the joined Portuguese and Aragonese at Zafra (3 August) and destroyed their remnants before Lisbon (10–11 September). Andalusīs are now 54% of the realm to the Castilians' 40%. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

Portugal made a separate peace on 11 September 1364 and gave up the Algarve and the lower Alentejo, thirteen towns, which the court means to make a vassal after the war. Saʿd is now called Conqueror and has a daughter by Aiman. The realm is 56 towns and 709,000 people, majority Catholic again with the Portuguese. Castile and Aragon fight on. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

The War of Independence is won. Granada has declared its independence. Castile gave up the land of Niebla and Huelva and pays reparations, as Portugal and Aragon do. The realm holds 62 towns and 732,000 people, and with its ṭāʾifas 61 of the Strait's 72. The treasury holds 1,131. The game put Granada back under Castile as a tributary after the peace, which Trent will remove with the console, so the chronicle and this snapshot treat Granada as independent. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

Six months after the Peace of Independence. The Ṭāʾifa of al-Gharb has been released, and the treasury of 1,131 has gone into the Great Madrasa of Ishbīliyya, the silver of Qusanṭīna and the farms of Úbeda. The game still lists Granada as Castile's tributary, which Trent removed with the console soon after; the chronicle treats Granada as free. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

Seven months after the Peace of Independence. Granada has no overlord, and the Portuguese south is now the Ṭāʾifa of al-Gharb. The army is stood down and the budget balances. A Great Madrasa is rising at Ishbīliyya. Saʿd has a son and heir, Ismāʿīl, by Duʿāʾ. Sunnīs and Catholics are exactly even. The alliance with the Mamlūks, in force since 1349, has lapsed since April. The Marīnids still hold the Strait's north shore. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

A year of peace. The Mamlūk alliance was renewed on 30 January 1367 and Castile is courting Granada's favour. A week ago Fās took up its claim to Granada's submission again. The treasury has run down to 87 while the building goes on. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

Three days after Morocco insulted Granada's envoys and gave it a casus belli of its own. Sunnīs now outnumber Catholics, 315,000 to 306,000, and Gharnāṭa's cloth guild has grown to its ninth level. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

wars: The Second Marīnid War for the Submission of Granada
coins.note: Morocco declares war to demand Granada's submission, with Tlemcen, Tafilalt, Touat and the puppet Kingdom of Sevilla. Granada has its three ṭāʾifas, and the Mamlūks and their vassals are allies again since January 1367. Sunnīs outnumber Catholics again, 317,000 to 305,000. Castile has closed its markets and guaranteed al-Gharb's independence. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

coins.t: A year of the Second Marīnid War
wars: The Second Marīnid War for the Submission of Granada
coins.note: A year into the Second Marīnid War. After the first winter's conquests on the north shore, the Moroccan counterattack has taken back all of it but Niebla. Khālid's army, half of it mercenaries paid with loans from the estates, held at Antequera and Almuñécar, and the first Mamlūk troops have landed at Gérgal. Expenses are more than double income. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

coins.t: The Peace of the North Shore
coins.save: SP_GRA_1370_09_13 (the second of the two; compressed)
coins.note: The Second Marīnid War is won. Morocco gave up the whole north shore, Ronda, Marbella and the so-called Kingdom of Sevilla, and with its ṭāʾifas Granada holds every town of the Strait's three lands. The war cost about 14,000 men on Granada's side and 23,000 on Morocco's. The estate loans are still owed. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

coins.t: The War of the Upper March
wars: The War of the Upper March
coins.note: On 1 December 1373 Granada declares war on Aragon under the Reconquest of Iberia claim, six months after the truce ran out. Aragon fights with only the crown its king also wears, Sicily, and Sicily's three subjects; Sicily's allies Genoa (at war with Bologna and Pisa since May) and the Pope stay out. The Mamlūks answer the call with their vassals, their galleys pointed at Sicily (Trent's account). The sultan leads the regulars himself and raises no levies: 3,300 men under arms against Aragon's 400. The debts are paid, the treasury holds 344, and the Castilian truce holds until June 1375. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

coins.t: The Peace of the Upper March
coins.note: On 15 March 1375 the War of the Upper March ends. Aragon gives up all 34 towns it still held, from the Pyrenees to the Ebro, and holds no land; Malta goes to the Mamlūks, and Sicily pays reparations. The realm grows from 60 towns to 94 and from 765,000 people to 1,275,000. The Catalans are now its largest people and Catholics outnumber Muslims two to one. The army of 3,300 regulars is whole, no levies were raised, and the treasury holds 286. New truces run with Sicily and its subjects to April 1386 and with Aragon to March 1388; the Castilian truce ends on 5 June 1375. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

On 16 March 1375 the sultan reorders the realm and proclaims the Restoration of al-Andalus. Murcia's twelve towns pass directly to the crown and its heir Bernarda is betrothed to Prince Ismāʿīl. The conquered lands of Aragon become two ṭāʾifas: Catalonia (28 towns around Barcelona) and a renewed Aragon (6 towns around Benabarre). Granada becomes al-Andalus (the game's ADU; the campaign keeps the realm as GRA), with the rank of an empire. The sultan chooses the convivencia: the Ornament of the World runs for 30 years. The crown holds 72 towns and 874,000 people, Muslims a majority again; its four ṭāʾifas hold 64 more. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

coins.t: The War of the Aragonese Restoration
wars: The War of the Aragonese Restoration
coins.note: On 5 June 1375, the day the Castilian truce runs out, al-Andalus declares war on Castile under the Reconquest of Iberia claim, framed as the restoration of Aragon. With France pushing England into the sea, the Emperor will not wait for Rome to rally the French. A levy of gold and men on the nobles and the ṭāʾifas fills the treasury: 1,579 against 286 in March. Portugal and the Papal States join Castile; the Mamlūks and the four ṭāʾifas join al-Andalus. At the declaration al-Andalus has 3,300 regulars and 4 ships against Castile's 1,750 men, Portugal's 1,050 and Rome's 684; the Mamlūks have 3,930. Maryam has sat in the dīwān since 17 March. The game now ranks al-Andalus 13th among the powers. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

On 6 April 1378 Castile and Portugal make peace. The Aragonese heartland, 24 towns with Zaragoza, is restored to the Ṭāʾifa of Aragon, which grows to 30 towns; 46 towns of the Middle and Lower Marches, with Toledo, Badajoz and Mérida, pass to al-Andalus; Castile pays reparations and falls from 229 towns to 159. The crown now holds 118 towns and 1,287,000 people. Castilians are again its largest people and Catholics outnumber Muslims, 713,000 to 503,000. The mercenaries still cost dearly: 133 a month out against 80 in, with 1,016 in the treasury. Truces run with Castile, Portugal and Rome to April 1393. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

By the end of November 1379 the capital has moved from Gharnāṭa to Ishbīliya, decided by the Jamāʿa in April. New roads tie the city to Sharīsh, Mālaqa, Baṭalyaws and Ṭulayṭula, paid for with five loans from the estates (565 in all); seven stretches are finished. The crown's grip on Seville has risen from 60% to 67%; it will take years to spread. The whole dīwān is integrating the new lands. The game recorded no historical capital at Gharnāṭa. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

On 4 March 1394 al-Andalus declares war on Castile under the Reconquest of Iberia, the third war of the Istirdād, with Morocco, the Mamlūks and the four ṭāʾifas; Portugal, Rome and Andorra stand with Castile's new king Pedro. Since 1379: the capital at Ishbīliya, the Toledan and Teruel risings crushed, the Hajj made at the second attempt, and the bureaucracy grown to three offices. The realm has 118 towns and 1,438,000 people; the game ranks it ninth. Prestige stands at 95 and the treasury at 568, with 565 still owed to the estates. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

At the Peace of Ramaḍān, 22 June 1395, Castile surrenders the War of the League at +100%, and Portugal follows: the third war of the Istirdād ends. Castile gives up 51 towns, Madrid, Salamanca, Ávila, Cuenca and Cáceres among them, and pays reparations for ten years; Portugal gives up 20, Lisbon, Setúbal, Santarém and Évora among them. All 71 pass to the crown: the realm grows from 118 towns to 189 and from 1,291,000 people to 2,334,000, and Catholics now outnumber Sunnis three to one. The game ranks it twelfth, down from ninth at the declaration. The treasury stands at 235, with 565 still owed to the estates. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

On 5 August 1395 two new ṭāʾifas are carved from the lands won at the Peace of Ramaḍān and given to the Emperor's cousins, sons of his late uncles: Shalamanka (21 towns of the Leonese west) to Saʿd ibn Ismāʿīl, and Qūnka (20 towns of the Castilian east) to Saʿd ibn Faraj, the Emperor's son-in-law. Madrid, Cáceres and all the Portuguese lands stay with the crown. The realm holds 148 towns and 1,742,000 people directly, with six ṭāʾifas; the game ranks it seventh. The treasury stands at 158, with 565 still owed; stability has fallen to 9.5. The same day the Dīwān al-Inshāʾ completes the bureaucracy. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

On 1 February 1404 the Pope proclaims the first crusade against al-Andalus and declares war on the Ṭāʾifa of Aragon; the Emperor answers for his subject, with the Mamlūks, Morocco and all six ṭāʾifas beside him. Against him stand the Papal States, Faenza, Siena and a few German princes, some 5,100 men. Since 1395: the two ṭāʾifas of Shalamanka and Qūnka, the Dīwān al-Inshāʾ, the Highland Survey's silver and iron, the burghers' privileges and the jewellers' charter. The realm holds 148 towns and 1,833,000 people; the game ranks it fourth. Income 200 a month against 165; the treasury stands at 51, with 565 still owed. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

On 22 October 1404 the Pope ends his crusade: his army destroyed by the Emperor at Barjols and Avignon itself taken, he is humiliated before Christendom and pays 585 in gold and reparations. No land changes hands. The French, who opened the road to Avignon, now also give food access. The court is already preparing a new claim on Castile. The realm holds 148 towns and 1,841,000 people; the game ranks it sixth. Income 209 a month against 178; the treasury stood at 45 before the gold came in, with 565 still owed. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

Ten weeks after the Peace of Avignon the conquered north rises: a Kingdom of Estremadura in the Portuguese lands, a Kingdom of Toledo again in La Mancha and the Madrid country, and Ciudad Rodrigo against the Ṭāʾifa of Shalamanka. Al-Andalus holds 100 towns of 148 and 1,295,000 people; Toledo, Lisbon and Setúbal hold. The rebels raise some 11,000 men, nearly all levies, against 3,400 regulars. The treasury stands at 218 with the Pope's gold. A rebellion, not a new border: the map shows the risings as they stood. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

On 2 March 1405 the Emperor Saʿd died on the march through Moya, and his son Ismāʿīl, thirty-eight, became Emperor and Sultan of al-Andalus; sixteen days later he broke the Kingdom of Toledo's army before Qūnka. By the law of primogeniture his heir is his eldest son Muḥammad, twenty, with the able Saʿd, twelve, behind him. His brother Yūsuf takes his old seat in the dīwān. The risings of 807 go on: al-Andalus holds 100 towns and 1,284,000 people directly. Treasury 291, income 217 against 177; 35 regiments in the field. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

The north is the crown's again. The rising of Ciudad Rodrigo ended on 8 July 1405, six days after Khālid ibn Yaḥyā's victory at Granadilla, and the Kingdom of Toledo and Estremadura collapsed on 24 August 1405, giving the crown back its forty-eight towns. On 1 September 1405 the Ṭāʾifa of al-Gharb was taken into the crown. The crown now holds 161 towns and 2,018,000 people directly, with five ṭāʾifas under it; Maryam bint Saʿd, the Emperor's niece and wife of his son Saʿd, has ruled Qūnka since her father's death in February 1408. In March 1408 the Emperor kept his court at Ishbīliya but named Qurṭuba the Capital of the Old Caliphate. The heir Muḥammad, twenty-two, has two gifted sons, Ismāʿīl and Aḥmad, both five, enough to set aside the question of the succession. Treasury 418, income 270 against 192; 9 regiments. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

On 29 June 1410 the truce of the Peace of Ramaḍān ran out and the Emperor Ismāʿīl declared war on Qashtāla for the rest of the peninsula, the fourth war of the Istirdād, which he named the War of Jillīqiya. Portugal joined Qashtāla; Fās, with Tilimsān and Tafilalt, answered the Emperor's call, and the Mamlūks were not needed. Al-Andalus, fifth among the powers of the world, holds 161 towns and 2,040,000 people directly, with five ṭāʾifas; Qashtāla has 108 towns and 2,033,000 people, Portugal 34 towns. At the declaration the Emperor had 4,900 regulars and 53 ships against Qashtāla's 1,650 and 25 and Portugal's 750 and 8. Treasury 386, income 274 against 238. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

On 1 November 1411 (14 Rajab 814) the War of Jillīqiya, the fourth war of the Istirdād, ended with the Peace of Rajab. Portugal was annexed whole and Qashtāla gave up 63 towns, Old Castile, León and Navarre; what is left of Qashtāla, 45 towns, is ruled from Oviedo. The conquests were given out at once as four new ṭāʾifas: Burtuqāl (the old Portugal) to the Emperor's cousin Aḥmad, Liyūn to the Emperor's son Aḥmad, Burghush (Old Castile) to Khālid ibn Yaḥyā Raḥḥū, and Banbalūna (Navarre) to the Emperor's cousin Yūsuf. The crown keeps 161 towns and 2,042,000 people, with nine ṭāʾifas under it. Europe is horrified, all but Paris. Treasury 816, income 220 against 303. Shares of power are estimated from the 1 June 1349 reading.

On 24 October 1414 (9 Shaʿbān 817) a Jamāʿa took the empire's mercenary contracts from the umarāʾ, passed a law to curtail them, and bought their votes with estates in the north that made them landlords, not lords. Wrapped in the Umayyad order of the kūras and the new doctrine of the sovereign, it left the nobles near-mutinous, one in ten content, and the realm shaken. The crown holds 162 towns and 2,078,000 people, with nine ṭāʾifas; Abū Ḥammū has ruled Burghush since his father Khālid's death in 1412. Treasury 697, income 284 against 239. Shares of power are estimated from the 31 December 1415 reading.

The estates panel of 31 December 1415, read the day before this save: the crown holds about a quarter of the power of the state, the dhimmī 22%, the burghers 19%, the umarāʾ 18%, the ʿulamāʾ 10%, the commoners 2%, and the tribes, new with the Canaries, under 1%. Fourteen months after the Jamāʿa the umarāʾ are a quarter content and recovering, with Prince Yūsuf appeasing them in the dīwān. On 11 June 1415 the Ṭāʾifa of Shalamanka was taken into the crown after its ruler's death, and Maxorata in the Canaries was settled. The crown holds 184 towns and 2,445,000 people directly, with eight ṭāʾifas. Treasury 1,923, income 251 against 232; the realm's peace is still shaken.

Ten days after Balansiyya was taken into the crown (1 August 1420) and the day after Fermoselle, where the Emperor destroyed the rising of Zamora. The crown holds 186 towns and 2,434,000 people directly, with seven ṭāʾifas: sixteen of Shalamanka's towns went to Liyūn and Burghush in November 1416, and Angra in the Azores was settled on 1 August. Estates are estimated from the reading of 31 December 1415: the crown about a quarter, the umarāʾ and the burghers a fifth each, the dhimmī 17% (lower now that Balansiyya's Muslims are the crown's), the ʿulamāʾ 12%. The umarāʾ are two in five content again. The treasury, 1,923 in 1416, is down to 277 with 565 owed, after the universities and the road to Balansiyya; income 260 against 236. Stability is barely above nothing, 5. The realm stands third in the world.

coins.t: The Petty Kings of the Mountains
coins.note: Twenty-four days after Balansiyya: on the day of this save the Kingdom of Qashtāla fell apart into Galicia (23 towns), Asturias (8) and Navarre (10, the Basque coast), leaving King Pedro four towns around Santander. Al-Andalus itself is unchanged: 186 towns of the crown and seven ṭāʾifas. Estates estimated from the reading of 31 December 1415. Treasury 306 with 565 owed; stability 6.

wars: The Mamlūk War on the Ottomans
coins.note: Five weeks after the Mamlūks went to war with the Ottomans, and a month after al-Andalus answered their call with all seven ṭāʾifas. The Ṭāʾifa of Burtuqāl has been the Kingdom of Portugal since 4 November 1421, still the Emperor's. Catalans and Sephardim are now accepted cultures beside the Portuguese. The crown holds 189 towns, with new settlements on Gran Canaria, the Cape Verde islands and Flores. Estates estimated from the reading of 31 December 1415. Treasury 232 with 565 owed; stability 17.

Six days after the Ottomans made peace with the Mamlūks and gave up thirty-seven towns of central Anatolia; al-Andalus fought no battles and took nothing. The crown holds 189 towns and 2,495,000 people, with seven ṭāʾifas. Estates estimated from the reading of 31 December 1415. Treasury 172 with 565 owed; income 306 against 257; stability 20.

The day of the Jamāʿa of 831, which revoked the Primacy of Nobility. The umarāʾ are one in six content and the realm's peace is all but gone (stability 1). The crown holds 194 towns and 2,552,000 people, with armouries in ten of its cities and settlements now on four islands of the Azores, four of the Canaries and three of the Cape Verdes. Seven ṭāʾifas; Banbalūna has a new lord, Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf. The truce with Castile ran out in 1426, and Galicia has swallowed Asturias. Estates estimated from the reading of 16 November 1428, six months later, after the Primacy was gone. Treasury 201 with 565 owed; manpower full at 13,700.

The estates panel of 16 November 1428 (7 Ṣafar 832), read with every estate's power tooltip on the day of this save: the crown 29.5% of the power of the state, the burghers 21.4%, the umarāʾ 17.1%, the dhimmī 16.7%, the ʿulamāʾ 12.5%, the commoners 2.8%. Six months after losing the Primacy the umarāʾ are a third content and rising. The rural works of 1428 stand in the save: village granaries in 167 of the crown's 194 towns, 41 acequias, 7 windmills. Treasury 540 with 565 owed; income 356 against 279; stability 2; manpower 14,000 of 15,500.

A save for Europe: three days after the peace that ended the Hundred Years' War, Edward of England is king of France as well. English Toulouse holds Languedoc along the Pyrenees, beside the Ṭāʾifa of Catalonia, and England, Castile's one ally, is the second power of the world. Al-Andalus is unchanged: 194 towns, seven ṭāʾifas, third in the world with 108 points. Estates estimated from the reading of 16 November. Treasury 611 with 565 owed; stability 2; manpower 14,100 of 15,700.

Four days after the Emperor Ismāʿīl II died in camp at Ishbīliya, on 28 June 1429, after twenty-four years on the throne. His son Muḥammad V, forty-three, reigns; the heir is Muḥammad's eldest son Ismāʿīl, and Ismāʿīl and his brother Aḥmad now sit in the dīwān. The succession has cost the crown most of its political influence (22, from 100). The crown holds 195 towns and 2,571,000 people, with seven ṭāʾifas; Teguise on Lanzarote was settled on 1 July. The Angevin Empire, Castile's ally, is second in the world with 180 points to al-Andalus's 101. Estates estimated from the reading of 16 November 1428. Treasury 647 with 565 owed; income 280 against 295; stability 6.

The day al-Andalus declared war on Galicia, the fifth war of the Istirdād, steered there by the two princes when their father wanted Castile. All seven ṭāʾifas march with the crown; Galicia, 31 towns and no army, stands alone. The crown holds 196 towns and 2,585,000 people (São Nicolau in the Cape Verdes settled on 1 January). Muḥammad V's first year: political influence back to 42, stability 9, the umarāʾ two in five content. Estates estimated from the reading of 16 November 1428. Treasury 591 with 565 owed; income 280 against 291; manpower 17,000 of 18,800.

The day of the declaration on Navarre, with Galicia beaten but not yet at peace: Santiago taken and its cathedral destroyed, the last Galician army wiped out at Oviedo. Navarre and Castile have no men under arms; the Angevin Empire, Castile's ally, stays out. The crown holds 196 towns, seven ṭāʾifas march with it, and stability has fallen below nothing (−0.4) with the new war. Estates estimated from the reading of 16 November 1428. Treasury 581 with 565 owed; manpower 17,300 of 19,000.

The day of the two peaces, 16 Ṣafar 834, after the battle before Bilbao. Galicia, beaten at 82 war score, is annexed whole; Navarre and Castile, at 59, go with it, and the Kingdom of Castile is no more. For the length of this save the crown holds 241 towns and 3.37 million people, from the Algarve to San Sebastián, before the north is handed out. Seven ṭāʾifas, no wars, stability 0.6. Estates estimated from the reading of 16 November 1428. Treasury 753 with 565 owed.

Two days after the Peace of Ṣafar the conquered north is settled. Old Asturias goes to Liyūn (now 35 towns), Cantabria to Burghush (38) and the Basque coast to Banbalūna (28), and the other 23 towns of Galicia, from Santiago, are made a ṭāʾifa again under Diego Sotomaior, a Galician Muslim. The crown keeps 196 towns and 2.59 million people; eight ṭāʾifas hold 236 towns and nearly 4 million more. The whole peninsula belongs to the Emperor and his ṭāʾifas, and the courts of the world rank the empire third, behind al-Ṣīn and the Angevins. Estates estimated from the reading of 16 November 1428. Treasury 753 with 565 owed.

The day the Pope proclaims the second crusade against al-Andalus, sparked by the destruction of Santiago, and declares war on the Ṭāʾifa of Aragon. Every ally answers: eight ṭāʾifas, the Mamlūks, Morocco and Tunis. The Emperor has embraced the name of warmonger that his enemies gave him in June. Stability has recovered to 4 and prestige to 82; the courts of the world still rank al-Andalus third. Treasury 784 with 565 owed. Estates estimated from the reading of 16 November 1428.

Seven months into the Crusade of 835. The war has been fought at sea and in Italy and Sardinia by the allies' fleets and armies; al-Andalus's own army hasn't fought, and the war score stands at 4 in the allies' favour. Seven arsenals and seven war galleys are under construction. The four Cape Verde towns have just become a colonial dominion, leaving the crown 192 towns. Stability 6.2, prestige 96, treasury 1,878 with 565 owed. Estates estimated from the reading of 16 November 1428.

The morning of the peace that ended the second crusade, at war score 5. The Pope, fighting Milan and Mantua as well, sues for terms. He will pay reparations and break with Genoa, Siena and Aquileia, and no land changes hands, so there is no save after the peace. The arsenals are still building. Stability 6.8, prestige 96, treasury 1,520 with 565 owed. Estates estimated from the reading of 16 November 1428.

Three years after the crusade. The arsenals are finished and eight Andalusī war galleys have joined the fifty caravels, and the realm's temper has moved far toward the sea. The Emperor has made the Hajj, given the realm a Ṣūfī Shaykh al-Islām, and rules Burghush as regent for a boy. Stability 17.6, the highest yet, prestige 90, income 396 against 305 spent, treasury 1,282 with 565 owed. The realm is at peace, and the courts of the world still rank it third. Estates estimated from the reading of 16 November 1428.

Catalonia is in the crown (221 towns, 3.25 million people), the realm's temper has tipped from the land to the sea for the first time, and harbours are rising in the Catalan ports. The Emperor's grandson Yūsuf, sixteen and thrice married, is made admiral of the fleet. Burghush has its own lord again, and the Emperor's mother Bernarda has died. Stability 24.2, the highest yet, treasury 1,653 with 565 owed, and the New World institution was born in Ishbīliya. Estates estimated from the reading of 16 November 1428.

Ten days after the Jamāʿa of 846 seated the burghers as equals. The princes have rallied the commoners and affirmed the ʿulamāʾ's rights, and the realm's peace holds at 14, but only the burghers are content (74); the umarāʾ (32), commoners (34), ʿulamāʾ (44) and dhimmī (45) are angry. The nobles' Land Rights are gone and the burghers hold Shipwright Contracts and Urban Development Grants. The realm's temper is now firmly seaward (+26). Treasury 1,767 with 565 owed. Estate power estimated from the reading of 16 November 1428.
